outcome: Stanley Yao Xiao posted a preprint in December 2024 (revised through June 2025) claiming a complete proof that five integer squares with constant second difference 2 must be consecutive, which would resolve Büchi's problem (with M=5); as of this research the paper has not been accepted by a journal or worked through by an expert digestion, so it remains a claim rather than a settled resolution.
summary: Büchi's problem (the 'n squares problem') asks for the least M such that every sequence of M or more integer squares with constant second difference 2 must be a sequence of consecutive squares; it was known that M ≤ 5 works unconditionally is the target (Büchi/Vojta-type results had reduced this to needing M=5, with M=4 known to fail in general and various partial/conditional results existing before the frozen date). On 21 December 2024, Stanley Yao Xiao posted arXiv:2412.16740, 'Hilbert's tenth problem for systems of diagonal quadratic forms, and Büchi's problem,' which the abstract and body present as completing the proof that any five squares x1²,...,x5² with second differences all equal to 2 must be consecutive — i.e., establishing the M=5 case unconditionally, which is the statement of Büchi's problem as it is generally posed. The paper has gone through at least three arXiv revisions, the latest (v3) dated 7 June 2025, indicating active revision consistent with a claim still being refined rather than a finished, community-vetted proof. I checked the paper itself (via fetch), the live Wikipedia article on Büchi's problem, and searched for any journal acceptance, expert blog digestion (e.g. Terence Tao's blog, Quanta, or a number-theory survey), or peer-reviewed publication announcement — none was found. The current Wikipedia article for Büchi's problem states explicitly: 'A positive answer was claimed in 2024 by Stanley Yao Xiao and is awaiting peer review as of July 2025,' which matches what I found independently. No expert digestion, journal acceptance, or formal verification (e.g. Lean/Coq) of the proof was located. I found no mention of AI, machine learning, or automated theorem-proving tools anywhere in the paper, in secondary coverage, or in searches combining Büchi's problem with AI/LLM terms — this appears to be conventional human mathematical work (analytic/algebraic number theory techniques building on Hilbert's Tenth Problem-style arguments). Given the proof is unrefereed and unreviewed by the expert community as far as I can determine, I classify this as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved,' with resolution_direction 'confirmed' since the claimed result, if correct, proves the conjectured statement (M=5 suffices) rather than refuting it.
competing_reading: One could argue for 'resolved' if journal acceptance or an expert digestion occurred that I could not find (e.g., paywalled venue, or a talk/seminar digestion not indexed by general web search — the paper has been presented, e.g. in a 'Number Theory Web Seminar' (NTWS 259) YouTube talk by Xiao, which is the author's own presentation, not an independent expert's verification). Absent an independent referee report or published acceptance, 'claimed' is the more conservative and, I believe, correct reading. It is also possible a case could be made that the problem, as most commonly stated with unspecified M, is only partially addressed (Xiao's result is specifically for the second-difference-2 case with M=5, which is the standard formulation of Büchi's problem, so I do not treat this as a mere 'case' or 'variant' — it directly targets the stated conjecture).
what_would_settle_it: Journal acceptance of arXiv:2412.16740 (or a successor version) at a peer-reviewed venue, or a public expert digestion (blog post, MathOverflow consensus, or citation in a survey) explicitly confirming the proof is correct and complete, would move this to 'resolved.' Conversely, a retraction, identified gap, or published counterexample to a lemma would move it to 'progress'/'incident.'

corrections.why: Reviewed and retained, WITH DOUBT. Scope is right: Xiao claims the M = 5 case, which is Buchi's problem as usually posed. Credibility is the open question. Against: an unconditional proof would be a major result (previous routes needed the Bombieri-Lang conjecture), and in almost two years it has drawn no expert engagement, no journal acceptance, and no mention in the live Wikipedia article. For: the author is an established number theorist working in exactly this area, the paper has been actively revised, and nothing has knocked it down. That falls short of the grounds used to set claims aside in the non-credible-claims batch, so it stays `claimed`. It is one of the rows a planned 'doubtful claim' marker is for.
